Good morning, everyone. We are team Four and Furious: Ayush Gupta, Harshita Gupta and Anushka Dixit. Our project is about finding cells, nerves and blood vessels in 3D microscope images, for the SELMA3D 2026 challenge. The images on the right show the problem: nobody labelled these types, and the blue areas are what our model found.

Here is the challenge. We got 3,400 images without labels, from 17 types of structures, to let the model learn on its own. But we got only 82 labelled images, from just six types. And the tricky part: 17 of the 26 test images show types that had no labels at all. So the real question is: can the model handle things it was never taught?

The labelled images come in two groups. Separate objects, like plaques and cells, are scored on whether each object is found. Connected structures, like vessels and nerves, are scored on whether the tubes stay connected. One model has to handle both.

This is our method. First, the model learns from the unlabelled images on its own. Then we train it on the 82 labelled images. Two trained models then work together, and we call this pair v15. For one entry, we also send tube-like images to two bigger models. Almost everything was trained on one laptop.

To learn from unlabelled images, we hide parts of an image and ask the model to fill them in. But these images are about 97 percent empty background, so we made the real structures count ten times more, and focused half of the training on them. The graph shows the model steadily improving.

Our first finding. The usual way to check a model uses labelled images of types it already knows. That check liked a model called v17, but on the real test v17 did worse. What really matched the test score, on the left, was simple: how much each model marks on the new types. Marking too much, like v11, or too little, like v17, both lowered the score. v15, in the middle, scored 0.616.

Our second finding. We hid two types during training and tested only on them. The longer we trained, the worse the model got on them. But it was not forgetting. If we tell the model how much to mark, the fully trained model is actually better. The real problem is the amount it marks: nerves three times too much, cells only half. Matching the amount to a steadier model, without labels, fixed most of it.

This idea shaped our second entry. Bigger models were better on nerves but worse on cells, so we made a simple rule that checks the shape of what was found. It got all 26 test images right. But the bigger models marked too little on new tube types. So the bigger models decide where the structure is, and v15 decides how much to mark.

Our third finding. We let the model learn a little from each test image, using its own confident guesses. On nerves, it helped in all six images. On cells, it made things worse in eight of nine. So this trick should only be used for tube-like structures.

Now our results. Connected structures, like vessels and nerves, are our strength: on the final test we scored 0.653 and 0.738, and the results were steady from image to image. Separate objects like cells were harder, at 0.547 and 0.360. Both our entries scored almost the same, so the credit goes to the v15 model.

Here is what the results look like. On the left, our predictions match the correct answers well. On the right, completely new types: nerves and vessels come out as connected networks, but faint cells are often missed.

That is where we still struggle. Out of more than 12,000 cells, only 39 percent were found, and they were drawn about half their real size. Faint cells were missed the most. So the problem is missing and shrinking cells.

To finish, three simple lessons. First, test your model on types it has never seen. Second, watch how much your model marks on new data, because too much or too little both cost points. Third, when a model gets worse on new types, it is often just marking the wrong amount, and that can be fixed without labels. Thank you. We are happy to take your questions.
